findings.title: `waiting` is set to a bare string, but `flow.py` reads it as a dict
quotes: sets `waiting` to `tests.suite not set` and stops (FR-35)
sets `waiting` to `T-n blocked after 3 attempts`
status, command = f"waiting_for_human: {state['waiting']['why']}", f"nio flow start {slug} --by human"
findings.fix: in CT-5, CT-9, CT-10 and CT-11, set `waiting` to `{"why": "<text>", "task": "T-n"}` (adding `change` in CT-11), the shape `stop_line` writes. Have CT-12 match on `waiting["task"]`.

sources.situation: the existing code always stores `waiting` as a dict. `stop_line` writes it with a `why` key, and `where`, `resumed` and `talk` read `state['waiting']['why']` and `waiting.get("change")`. CT-5, CT-9, CT-10 and CT-11 each say "sets `waiting` to `<text>`". Read literally, a string makes `where` raise TypeError on the first wait. CT-12's "clears `waiting` when it names this task" also needs a task key that no contract defines.

findings.reason: CT-5, CT-9, CT-10 and CT-11 say "sets `waiting` to <text>" and no contract defines the dict shape. `flow.py:645` reads `state['waiting']['why']`, so a bare string would raise. CT-12's "names this task" needs a task key that nothing defines.
findings.note: waiting is the dict flow.stop_line writes: why, plus task and change (CT-5, CT-9, CT-10, CT-11, CT-12)

findings.title: Task fields on history lines are dropped by `flow.record`
quotes: new line kinds, each naming its `task` (FR-18)
line = {"kind": e["kind"], "at": stamp.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"), "who": who, "from": e.get("from"),
if e.get("change") is not None:
findings.fix: say in architecture.md and the contracts that task fields go under `evidence` (or that `record` gains a `task` key), and that task lines carry `from`/`to` = `implementing`.

sources.situation: `record` builds each line from a fixed set of keys: `kind`, `at`, `who`, `from`, `to`, `evidence`, `run`, `state`, plus `reason` and `change`. Any other key on an entry is dropped. The contracts put `task`, `command`, `runner`, `frozen`, `failing` and `collected` on lines, but never say where they go. If they are top-level keys, CT-4's `status` can't tell which task a line is for. Nor does any contract say what `from`/`to` a task line carries. `last_to(lines)` feeds the next `back` or `resume` line's `from`, so a task line with `to: None` breaks that.

findings.reason: `flow.record` (flow.py:147-153) builds each line from a fixed key set (kind, at, who, from, to, evidence, run, state, reason, change) and drops anything else. architecture.md says only that lines "name their `task`" and CT-4 `status` depends on that. No contract says where `task` or the `from`/`to` of a task line go.
findings.note: task lines carry from/to implementing and their fields under evidence, which flow.record keeps (CT-4)

findings.title: CT-9 rolls back "from the index", not byte-for-byte as `commit_gate` does
quotes: restores `history.jsonl` and `state.json` from the index as they were before step 2
kept = hp.read_bytes() if hp.exists() else None
findings.fix: copy `commit_gate`. Save the bytes of `history.jsonl` and `state.json` and the `write-tree` before step 2, then write them back and `read-tree` on failure.

sources.situation: `commit_gate`, the code CT-9 names on its `Like:` line, keeps the files' bytes in memory before writing, then writes them back and runs `read-tree`. Under CT-9, history is only staged at a task's commit. So before step 2 the index holds the version from the previous task's commit, without this task's `claim`, `red`, `green` and `review` lines. Restoring from the index wipes them. The task can then no longer read `green` as FR-19 and AC-47 require.

The task's `claim`, `red`, `green` and `review` lines are written to `history.jsonl` during the task and are uncommitted until CT-9 step 3. In the CT-9 order, step 3 stages `history.jsonl` and `state.json` after step 2 has written `task_done`. A restore "from the index" then has two outcomes. If the index is the staged post-step-2 version, it still holds `task_done`, which breaks "no done line". If the index is the last commit, `git restore` drops every uncommitted `claim`/`red`/`green` line. Status then falls back to `ready`, not `green`, and the frozen hashes are lost. Either way AC-47's "status `green`" and "no done line" cannot both hold.

a pre-commit hook rejects `T-n: <title>`. If the files are restored from the index, they come back with the `task_done` line, because step 3 staged them after step 2. If they come from the index as it was before step 2, they come back as HEAD's copies, and the uncommitted `claim`, `red`, `green` and `review` lines of this task are lost. The task's lines can't be rebuilt, and nothing says the index is reset. TC-47 checks only the outcome (no `task_done` line, status `green`), so it doesn't prove the files come back byte for byte.

findings.reason: CT-9 restores "from the index", while `commit_gate` (flow.py:979-999), the code on CT-9's `Like:` line, restores the bytes it kept in memory and then runs `read-tree`. The task's `claim`/`red`/`green`/`review` lines are uncommitted before step 3, so an index-based restore is wrong.
findings.note: a failed commit writes back the bytes kept before the done line and read-trees the saved tree, as commit_gate does (CT-9); TC-47 checks it

findings.title: A task blocked after 3 attempts tells the human to run `nio flow start`, which doesn't unblock it
quotes: `where` reports `waiting_for_human: <why>` from `state["waiting"]` as for other stages
return line, {**state, "pause": None, "abandon": None, "waiting": None}
findings.fix: in CT-14, when `waiting` names a blocked task, show `nio flow unblock <slug> T-n --human "<reason>" --by human` as the command (and C-record settlement for `cause: spec`). Add a matching row to `talk`.

sources.situation: CT-14 keeps `where`'s existing waiting branch, so the human is shown `nio flow start <slug> --by human`. `start` calls `resumed`, which clears `waiting` and writes a `resume` line, but the task stays `blocked`. The next claim then fails with "no ready task", and the human is never shown `nio flow unblock`, the command FR-38 makes for this.

findings.reason: CT-14 keeps `where`'s waiting branch, which prints `nio flow start <slug> --by human` (flow.py:645). `start` clears `waiting` but leaves the task blocked. Nothing in CT-14 or CT-12 points the human to `nio flow unblock`.
findings.note: where shows nio flow unblock for a blocked task and nio flow green after a failed commit (CT-14)

findings.title: The worker pack contradicts its own spec and the worker card
quotes: exactly these six parts, each under its own `## ` heading, in this order:
the pack's parts are exactly those five
- To go against an approved or current record, write a change request first (@nio:remember).
findings.fix: send a change request to AC-1 for the sixth part, or move the mode and handoff format into the card. Build part 1 without the `WORKER` block (or with a worker text that points to the blocked handoff). Nest `pack.build`'s headings under part 1.

sources.situation: CT-6 adds a sixth part (mode and handoff format) that AC-1's "exactly those five" forbids. Part 1 is `pack.build`'s output, which ends with its `WORKER` text. That text tells the worker to write a change request itself through `@nio:remember`. CT-15 and FR-23 instead tell it to stop and hand off `status: blocked` for the orchestrator to file with `nio flow block`. A worker handed this pack gets two different ways to report a spec problem. `pack.build` also emits its own `## ` headings, so "each under its own `## ` heading" no longer marks the parts.

findings.reason: AC-1 and FR-4 say "and nothing else", but CT-6 and TC-1 add a sixth part (mode and handoff format). Part 1 is `pack.build`, whose `WORKER` text (pack.py:19-22) tells the worker to write a change request itself, while CT-15 and FR-23 tell it to hand off `status: blocked`.
findings.note: the pack has five parts; pack.build's worker text is left out and its headings nested; mode and handoff format live in the card (CT-6, TC-1)

findings.title: A task whose commit failed is stuck at green with no event that moves it on
quotes: reject: review pending | ignore | → done
The task stays `green` (FR-19).
findings.fix: add a retry event to the `green` row and to CT-8/CT-9. For example, green on a `green` task re-runs the review and commit instead of `ignore`. Or add a `nio flow commit <slug> T-n` command.

sources.situation: A pre-commit hook rejects T-3's commit (AC-47). T-3 is `green`, the effort is waiting, and the human fixes the hook and runs `nio flow start`. The only events that can leave `green` are `review passes`, `review fails` and `spec problem filed`. `review passes` is only produced by an accepted green, and in the `green` row `green accepted` is `ignore`. CT-8 only accepts green on a `red` task, or on a `claimed` direct-mode task. So there is no command to retry the commit. `claim` is rejected (task already claimed) and `red` is rejected (review pending). The state is not final and cannot be left. The human can only abandon the effort or edit history by hand.

findings.reason: In the state table's `green` row, `green accepted` is `ignore`, `claim` is rejected and `red` is `reject: review pending`. The only exits are the review events and a spec problem. No event retries a failed commit, and CT-9 adds none.
findings.note: green on a green task re-runs the review and commit, leaving through review passes or fails (CT-8)

findings.title: A failed unknown-runner baseline is never re-run, so the stage proceeds on a failing baseline
quotes: the first claim of the stage, when no `baseline` line exists, starts the stage in this order:
with an unknown runner and a non-zero exit, sets `waiting` to `the baseline fails and its runner is unknown` and stops (FR-36).
findings.fix: write the `baseline` line only when the baseline is usable, or add a `baseline_failed` marker. Alternatively make the stage start re-run until the latest baseline line is valid.

sources.situation: `tests.suite` is `python check.py`, an unknown runner, and it exits 1. Step 3 writes the `baseline` line, then step 4 sets `waiting` and stops. The human fixes the suite and runs `nio flow start`. The next `nio flow claim` sees that a `baseline` line exists, so it skips the stage start. It claims T-1 without re-running the suite, on a recorded baseline that exited 1. At every review, "any non-zero suite exit at review is a new failure" (FR-36), so every review of that unknown-runner suite fails. The tasks burn their 3 attempts and end up blocked.

findings.reason: CT-5 starts the stage only "when no `baseline` line exists", but step 3 writes the baseline line before step 4 stops on an unknown runner with a non-zero exit. The next claim therefore skips the stage start and never re-runs the suite. CT-3 and FR-36 then treat every non-zero exit at review as a new failure.
findings.note: no baseline line is written while the baseline is unusable, so the next claim runs it again (CT-5)

findings.title: A pre-existing collection or import error in the baseline makes every later review fail
quotes: `broken` when the output shows a collection or import error marker (CT-2) or `cause` is set;
the suite (CT-3) with a failing name missing from the baseline, `broken`, a smaller `collected`
findings.fix: say what happens when the baseline is itself `broken`. Either wait for the human like FR-36, or compare collection errors by name against the baseline's.

sources.situation: At stage start the repo has a module that already fails to import. pytest exits 2 and prints `ERROR collecting ...`, and the baseline run has `broken: true`. CT-5 steps 3 and 4 only handle an unknown runner with a non-zero exit, so the baseline is recorded and the stage proceeds. Review rule 3 then fails on `broken` whenever the suite still shows that collection error, so T-1's review fails however correct T-1 is. Three attempts later T-1 is blocked. `unblock` resets the attempts but not the cause, so T-2 meets the same failure. The Review table separates "failure missing from the baseline" from "collection or import error" and gives no baseline carve-out for the second. FR-16 and AC-19 treat the baseline as tolerating pre-existing failures.

findings.reason: The Review table's third column and CT-8 rule 3 fail on any `broken` suite. Neither CT-5 nor CT-3 gives the baseline a carve-out for a pre-existing collection or import error, and CT-5 step 4 covers only the unknown-runner case. Every review would fail on a pre-existing import error.
findings.note: C-261029-kubi: Q29: a suite broken before the first task pauses the stage

findings.title: The Red decision table accepts a missing program on an unknown runner, and CT-7 gives no order that overrides it
quotes: | non-zero | unknown | - | accepted on the exit code alone | [human] |
a time limit or a missing program (CT-1) → `refused: <cause>`.
findings.fix: add the cause check to the Red decision table, or state in CT-7 that `cause` is checked before the exit code and `wrong_reason`.

sources.situation: Red runs `nosuchtool tests/test_x.py`. The runner is unknown and the exit code is 127, so the Red table's row 4 says `accepted on the exit code alone`. FR-44 and AC-49 say a missing program is refused. For a known runner whose binary is missing (`pytest tests/test_x.py` with pytest uninstalled), the output "command not found" matches none of the CT-2 error markers, and `wrong_reason` returns `""`. CT-7 lists the cause bullet last and does not say it is checked first. An implementation that follows the Red table and the CT-7 bullet order accepts red, freezes files and records a green-ready state for a command that never ran a test. The same gap exists for a timed-out command, where the code is `None`.

findings.reason: CT-7's `Fails:` list is a set of independent refusals, and the cause bullet ("a time limit or a missing program (CT-1) → `refused: <cause>`") needs no ordering to override the exit-code check. CT-1 sets `cause` for exit 127 regardless of runner, and FR-44 says "treat it as a refused red". The tension is with the spec's Red table row 4, which is a spec issue and not something the plan leaves open.

If they come from the index as it was before step 2, they come back as HEAD's copies, and the uncommitted `claim`, `red`, `green` and `review` lines of this task are lost. The task's lines can't be rebuilt, and nothing says the index is reset. TC-47 checks only the outcome (no `task_done` line, status `green`), so it doesn't prove the files come back byte for byte.

findings.title: Adding `Mode` to FIELDS strands every tasks.md approved before the change
quotes: `Mode` joins `FIELDS`.
planned tasks are frozen after approval
`mode` is `implement.mode` from the config when set, else the task's `Mode:` value (FR-40).
findings.fix: state the migration. Either require `Mode` only for tasks not yet frozen at approval and default a missing mode (for example `split`) in CT-4, or ignore the added `Mode:` line in the frozen-block comparison. Add a TC that claims a task from a `tasks.md` approved without `Mode:`, and say how the fixture and existing tests change.

sources.situation: an effort whose `tasks.md` was committed as `nio: approve tasks` before this change has no `Mode:` lines. `nio check tasks` now rejects every task with "needs `- Mode:`". Adding the lines makes `check_fixes` report "changed after `nio: approve tasks`". CT-4 gives no mode when the line is missing and `implement.mode` is unset. The effort can't move forward or be repaired without going back and re-approving. The shared fixture `tests/fixtures/tasks/tasks.md` also has no `Mode:` line (the `impl()` helper has to add it), so suites already using it may fail too. No TC covers a `tasks.md` approved before the change.

findings.reason: plan-risk-rollback: CT-4 defaults a missing mode to `split`, but CT-16's exemption depends on an approval commit that "predates this change", with no stated way for `check` to tell. No TC claims from a `tasks.md` approved without `Mode:`, because `impl()` always adds the line.
findings.note: the exemption is checkable: the approve commit's committer date before tasks.MODE_SINCE (CT-16); TC-56 claims from a list approved without Mode and checks a later one is refused

findings.title: Nothing says what happens to a blocked or failed task's uncommitted work
quotes: uncommitted changes outside `.nio/specs/<slug>/` → `error: uncommitted changes outside the effort folder:` and one line per file (FR-22)
then two greens with failing code
then claim, then red
findings.fix: name the rule. For example, `block` and the 3-attempt cap save the task's diff as a patch under the run folder, or stash it with a named stash, and then restore a clean tree. `unblock` leaves the tree clean. Add a TC that blocks a task, unblocks it, claims it again, and finds the saved diff.

sources.situation: a task blocked after 3 attempts (CT-10) or on a spec problem (CT-11) leaves its test and code edits uncommitted. Either CT-5 refuses the next claim, or the human discards the edits by hand, and the plan doesn't say whether they may be thrown away or must be kept. TC-36 claims right after unblocking TC-23's task, whose failing code is still in the tree, so as written it contradicts CT-5. FR-38's "next claim starts at the test phase" also implies the earlier work is dropped, with no recovery.

findings.reason: CT-5 refuses a claim when there are uncommitted changes outside the effort folder. A blocked task (CT-10, CT-11) leaves its edits uncommitted, and nothing says to save or discard them. TC-36 claims straight after unblocking TC-23's task, whose failing code is still in the tree, so it contradicts CT-5.
findings.note: Q28: a blocked task's edits are saved as a patch in the run folder and the tree cleaned (CT-10, CT-11)

findings.title: Stopping between the change record and the `blocked` line duplicates the record
quotes: 1. creates a change record (`records.new`, `outcome: pending`, `against` the effort's `spec.md`) holding the three parts;
When a `blocked` line for this task already carries that hash, nothing new is written
findings.fix: look up an existing pending change record holding the same handoff hash before calling `records.new`, or put the hash in the record and search for it. Add a TC that writes the record without the `blocked` line, runs `block` again, and expects one `C-*` file.

sources.situation: the record is written first, and the dedup hash only lives on the `blocked` line written in step 2. If `block` stops after step 1 (a crash, a lock takeover, a `flow.record` error), no line carries the hash. The retry creates a second pending `C-*` record for the same handoff, leaving an orphan that the human must decide or delete. TC-48 only covers two complete calls.

findings.note: the handoff hash is written into the change record and a pending record holding it is reused (CT-11)

- Tests: TC-38, TC-40
then red through the CLI with each.
- Action: claim; then green.
findings.fix: move TC-38 to US-2 and TC-40 to US-1, or split TC-38's `runner`/`wrong_reason` unit part into Foundation; move TC-35 to US-2.

sources.situation: Foundation runs TC-38 and TC-40. TC-38 runs red through the CLI (CT-7, delivered in US-2) and TC-40 claims (CT-5, delivered in US-1). TC-35 is in US-1 but runs green (CT-8, US-2). findings.title: TC-9's frozen file is committed before the claim, so CT-7 would freeze nothing

commits it all, and writes a `start` line through `test_flow.history`
